The study was published in the Journal of Aircraft, Vol. 49, No. 2, March-April 2012, by Chi H.E. Cheung and Kuen Y. Lin from the University of Washington.
Fasteners can completely stop Mode I crack propagation by providing a pivot that creates a closing moment at the crack tip.
In Mode II loading, fasteners cannot completely arrest propagation but can significantly retard it through three mechanisms: joint stiffness, fracture mode transition, and crack-face friction.
Mode II crack propagation begins as load is increased by 25-50% depending on clearance, layup, friction coefficient, and installation torque.
The finite element model used 2D four-node bilinear quadrilateral elements (CPEG4R) with one element per ply thickness of 0.1905 mm.
AS4/3501-6 carbon/epoxy material was used with Mode I fracture toughness G_IC = 262.7 J/m² and Mode II fracture toughness G_IIC = 1226 J/m².
The Benzeggagh-Kenane mixed-mode fracture law was applied with η = 1.75 for the composite material system.
Fastener joint stiffness was 24.72 kN/mm for quasi-isotropic layup and 33.67 kN/mm for 50%-0 degree layup.
A 0.1 mm fastener hole clearance allows the crack to advance more than 25 mm further than with perfect tolerance at 35 kN applied load.
The split-plate model was 203.2 mm long with an initial 50.8 mm crack and 3.048 mm thick plates.
Fastener springs were positioned 63.5 mm from the cracked end, with the initial 12.7 mm of crack propagation uninfluenced by the springs.
The width-to-diameter ratio of the test model was 5 using a 6.35 mm diameter fastener.
Layup configuration had no noticeable impact on fastener arrest effectiveness between quasi-isotropic and 50%-0 degree configurations.
The fracture mode transition mechanism provides a step increase in propagation load immediately when the crack reaches the fastener.
Crack-face friction effect is doubled because it simultaneously reduces axial load on one plate while increasing it on the other.
The elastic influence of the fastener preload extends more than 2 mm before the crack tip reaches the fastener.
Multiple fasteners increase arrest capability, with each fastener only increasing arrest capability after the crack reaches that fastener.
The study used automatic damping in Abaqus to aid convergence while limiting damping to avoid significant impact on solutions.
Thermal contraction due to curing was not simulated since the two plates were identical.
The fastener was modeled as a titanium Ti-Al6-V4 with elastic modulus of 113.8 GPa.
Crack bridging was not modeled, representing a conservative (non-optimistic) scenario for fracture toughness.
The finite bond layer was not explicitly modeled; crack propagation was assumed to occur when critical SERR was reached.
Installation torque and fastener hole clearance are critical parameters affecting arrest capability.
The study demonstrated that fasteners can be effective fail-safe features even when installed in bonded/cocured structures.
Fastener sizing involves tradeoffs between acceptable crack propagation and detrimental effects of the drilled hole on structural integrity.
